Coming from the pharmacy side, like you I've largely seen them as positive tools for our patients to use. We have safety and efficacy data going back well past a decade with numerous products, and the weekly dosing rotation is so much better for adherance than once daily shots, which especially for people who don't have good daily routines could become exhaustive. With their expansion into use as a direct weight loss aid, we can visibly see the benefits across most who take it. There are, however, a few caveats that have worried me.

1) Supply simply can't keep up with the demand. We have been in rotating outages of various types since the approval for weight reduction, and from people I've talked to it's not even due to supply being pinched or the like, manufacturing lines for these injectables are just that restrictive.  We were at an almost full outage at the start of the year, some are starting to bounce back as the companies producing them have doubled down, but that might not be a sustainable turnaround point and rotating outages might simply be the norm.  This makes dosing incredibly inconsistent, as people will switch from mounjaro to zepbound to trulicity based on availability and even within the same class doctors are reducing or increasing dosage based on supply, not medical analysis (right now 12.5 is in short supply, so doctors are writing for 10s).  This is not only not conducive for proper dosing of peoples medication, but it also increases the chance of dispension errors.  I've worked weekends where I look at a patients profile and see 12 different drugs/strengths prescribed or filled within the last 6 months and the patient themself doesn't know which one they're currently taking, and then get upset when I turn them away until I can unpluck this mess with the doctor the next day. Plus prior authorizations tend to be based on the drug, and in some cases even the strength. And of course, with supply issues comes adherence issues, as people have no alternatives or can't afford the $700+ out of pocket cost if their approved medication isn't available, so people are stopping coverage. Leading into

2) People are treating this as essentially chemical liposuction. Take it and done, you're healthy! You can lose dozens of pounds without changing your eating habits, your exercise habits, tending to your overall health, or anything!  Except that rapid weight loss can be problematic on its own, and if  there are any interruptions your body has established none of the routines that keep you from jumping right back, often with very unappealing fat distributions.  This process also stresses your pancreas, can be muscle wasting if you don't exercise leaving you without the benefits of a slow, sustained exercise associated weight loss to explore your new physical limitations, and has a host of other less likely problems that while unlikely become evident in such a huge patient population.  People aren't really engaging with their health in a holistic lens, but rather see this as a shot that allows them to continue the lives that led them here to begin with.  This becomes especially problematic when we get to 

3) a lot, and I mean a LOT, of the patients taking these injectables are doing it through tele-health and online services. Services that aren't there to discuss your overall health, to do careful testing, to keep up to date, and add an administrative expense to the existing costs (in addition to being mostly self pay driven).  Remote prescribing is overall good given the limitations of our health care system as it exists now, but people don't really realize that these services? They exist to sell you these products.  Unless you have a red flag in your health that would be prohibitive, they will get you an order for it. It doesn't really matter to them what your overall health profile looks like or what better options they would be.  And while we need more options for peoples healthcare, in this case it's at the cost of holistic care and careful monitoring.  

Overall, I'd rather we treated these drugs more like phentermine (well, phentermine before covid destroyed our standards of care).  Frequent checking of weight and side effects, association with specialists who have experience with weight loss as a whole, more prescription guidelines, etc. It's a very odd world where I see some insurance companies doing the right thing in requiring enrollment and engagement in weight watchers for a prior authorization.   These drugs are marvelous and beneficial for so many of our patients, but we have to find a way to back up from the rapidfire rate at which they're being thrown out and we have to reframe how they fit into our patients overall health.

Zepbound is a recently approved weight loss medication containing tirzepatide, a dual GLP-1 and GIP receptor agonist. It is designed to help adults with obesity or overweight conditions, especially those with related health complications like type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular diseases.

- Enhance insulin secretion post-meal, aiding in better glycemic control.

Now for the darker part: post-weight loss depression and suicide. 

This is something they warn you about when you sign up to get bariatric surgery. I wish they had done it in the late 90s/early 00s when I first dropped a bunch of weight because it's REAL. When you lose a lot of weight, it comes with a massive surge of hormones and emotions. 

Fat stores estrogen for both sexes, so if you drop a bunch of weight in a short period of time and suddenly feel insane, it's not all in your head. Your hormones are off-the-chain, most likely. A lot of bariatric patients report seriously disturbed emotions in the three months immediately after surgery. It usually settles after about a year, but it can be severe for some people, and if you're doing a major weight loss program, make sure you're taking this into account. 

For binge eaters that get bariatric surgery, you're taking away their crutch. I am a binge eater with an extremely addictive personality. One of the craziest things I ever came face-to-face with was the fact that my overeating was 98% mental. I had a real come-to-Jesus moment about three weeks after I had surgery. It was a real mourning as the realization hit that I am never going to be able to comfort myself with food again. I say without exaggeration that it felt like having some sort of exorcism. It was that emotional, but it was worth it. 

Another thing that people REALLY struggle to come to terms with is that society as a whole and individuals will consider you more lovable once you are a normal weight. You will get more dates. You'll turn more heads. Have better job prospects. People will treat you better. The likelihood that you will resent is high because you will perceive yourself as being as the same person you always were. You will feel a lot of anger around it, most likely, even if you rationally understand the why, and suddenly all of that attention you were getting may feel insulting. 

"Oh, I wasn't good enough - I wasn't enough - when I was a size 18? And now that I'm a 6/8, I'm the perfect girl? Fuck off!" 

There is also the cohort of people that will neg you for losing weight or the way that you lost it. Whether you have bariatric surgery, inject Ozempic or Mounjaro, go keto, or decide to just eat less and walk more, people will give your their opinion on your methods. I did a doctor-supervised very low calorie diet (VLCD) in high school, and a family member was ballsy enough to tell me that she thought it was better that I be heavy than do that. (She weighed probably 450-500 lbs. and died younger than she needed to because of it.)

It's a good idea to get a therapist when you start losing a lot of weight. Most people that have been heavy for a long time aren't prepared for what's coming. I do not have a therapist and probably ought to get one, but I really wish I'd had one when I was 16 and losing tons of weight and had NO IDEA why my brain was in full revolt or how to deal with the way people were treating me. 

If anyone reads this that is losing weight and struggling, call your doctor. It's common to feel all kinds of ways about major life changes like this, and it's normal to need help reframing deeply ingrained habits and life patterns. It's far better to acknowledge the struggle and ask for help than let the demon win.

I'll talk about this a little more. I've been thru enough weight loss programs that I can speak to it a little. 

First of all, when you start losing large amounts of weight and get more attractive to more people, you get hit on more. I've experienced it before. Everyone likes attention. If you have a spouse who has grown indifferent for whatever reason, it's easy to understand why someone new would hold a lot of allure. 

Sometimes you have a case where the spouse has issues with control, jealousy, etc. Sometimes they can't handle the attention that the newly slender partner is getting. My opinion is that this could be remedied by stepping up their own game, but not everyone is ready, willing, and able to do that. Some people actually prefer a heavier partner. 

Probably the biggest and most important thing is that, when you've been heavy for a long time or even most of your life, you have to realize that Fat You might not be the Real You. They say money is the root of all evil, but I say that it only amplifies that was already there. It's the same with beauty. Sometimes people lose weight, and their personality changes. They may not be as motivated to be nice or forgiving or whatever because they have realized (correctly) that they have more options. They may also be discovering things that they "liked" were really things that they were settling for. They may be discovering a whole new set of likes and dislikes that ends up resulting in a whole new lifestyle that the old partner just isn't adapted to. 

I don't even necessarily think this is all bad. I think we should change as we find that we can do more and get more from life. What you don't want to see is that someone's personality does a total 180, but it can and does happen. 

At the end of the day, if you have made changes that are entirely for the better for your health, and your partner can't support that or wants you to stay shut away to dull your shine, they probably aren't the one for you, anyway. Our partners should be our biggest cheerleaders.

1. The drugs are GLP-1 receptor AGONISTS. They don't activate or inhibit anything.

2. GLP-1 is a naturally produced hormone from the intestines but is metabolized in minutes. 

3. GLP-1 has numerous beneficial effects, including, and most especially, slowing the intestines (making people feel more full for longer) and activating satiety signals in the brain (making people experience less hunger). 

True!

4. The slowing of the intestines, in addition to reducing hunger, has an effect of substantially increasing nausea. Also, this can be so strong that some people die from the intestines slowing too much, which is lethal. 

Not true! Gastroparesis is extremely rare, and non lethal. The increase in nausea is due to *where* in the brain the GLP-1 receptors are targeted. Drugs like Mounjaro have significantly less nausea.

5. This nausea can become so problematic, that 70% of users chose to stop the drug of their own volition at 2 years of use. 

Not true! Users quit due to lack of enjoyment for food, not nausea.

6. Even those who continue the drug through two years, the benefits start to diminish, with a complete return of cravings to sweet foods. 

True. However most drugs require chronic usage. 

7. A substantial amount (~40%) of the weight lost while taking the drug is from fat-free mass, including muscle and bone. 

True, but this can happen with any rapid weight loss. This can be avoided with adequate strength training and protein intake.

I think the socratic framing is useful here:

Addiction can express itself two ways: as a disorder of the lower mind, and as one of the higher mind:

In the former case, the cause is incidental, and local to the neural network in question, neural adaptation to a long term lack of stimulation, genetic predispositions, the likes..

But in the latter case, no local root cause can be identified because it is a disorder of compatibility - the agent cannot find a viable configuration within its local environment, and cannot escape its local environment, thus, the decision is made to temporarily increase entropy in hopes that a viable configuration might emerge.

Now, initially, the brain can do this by itself - prolonged states of high uncertainty are generally associated with higher neural entropy
- Carhart-Harris et al. (2014)
- Obligatory Friston et al.
but it doesn't seem to take too long for the brain (the organ) to admit defeat and pass the task of increasing available entropy to the mind.

That's what I mean when I talk about the pull of altered states of consciousness, and what I mean when I say real addiction isn't physical.

Because, while it might then progress to neuronal adaptation as mentioned in our former case, the underlying cause is still not within our local scope, will never be within our local scope, and won't ever change to be compatible with the local scope. (momentum is too high at this point, our control systems have ruled out a pivot centuries ago)

This is one of those issues where you genuinely can't imagine or empathize unless you've experienced it. And I mean it, genuine, real addiction. Not recreational drug use that gets a little out of hand, not the occasional bender.. this is an extreme state that a functional mind can't and shouldn't be able to emulate / "imagine"

And, as much as it hurts me to say this, it's one of those issues where trying to help without deeply understanding it has caused so much harm, and will cause so much more.

I guess what I'm really trying to say here is that the existence of local solutions for non-local problems is a tautological impossibility, and that any claimed local "solution" can never be more than a symptomatic treatment.

And masking the symptoms is only going to make the problems worse.

I enjoy your writing, and there are a few things that I think you should consider.

First, obviously, I agree that if people can control any symptom -- obesity, allergies, heart disease risk, mood, attention, whatever -- without medicine, that's ideal! A top pharmaceutical researcher once told me that drugs don't so much fix things as break something else.

But that doesn't change the fact that biology is imperfect and unfair and many people need medicines. (At the extreme: you wouldn't treat cancer or type 1 diabetes with diet.)

Also, we do live in an unhealthy environment that encourages obesity, diabetes. If we can figure out regulatory steps to change that I'd be for it! And maybe there is a Nixon going to China element to that happening in a Trump administration.

But what doesn't follow is your implication that the GLP-1 analogues should not be widely used because people should try diet and exercise first.

First, because many of them have tried diet and exercise. In the trials of tirzepatide, a newer GLP-1, the placebo group was counseling on diet and exercise, and people in the placebo group lost 3% of their body weight. People in the drug group lost 20%.

In people with high cardiovascular risk who were obese but not diabetic, Ozempic reduced the rate of heart attacks and strokes. These drugs are also having a positive impact on things like knee arthritis and sleep apnea.

Now, I'd agree that it's probably true that people who don't really need Ozempic will get it and those who really need it won't. That's the fundamental problem in American medicine, it's true of heart stents, its true of antidepressants -- just about everything.

But I'd also point you to the experience with statin drugs. A lot of people who eat healthy diets and exercise frequently still have high LDL. The data are pretty clear that these medicines are safe for most people and will reduce their risk of heart attacks. Do you really think people shouldn't take them? Statins are cheap and a pill.

And this is the problem with a lot of this discussion. Of course we need to be careful with diet, of course we need to watch overmedication.

But data from randomized controlled trials also indicates these new drugs could save lives if we use them correctly -- and doing that will still mean they need to be given to a lot of people.

_ The SUMMIT clinical trial, conducted at 146 sites in the United States and internationally, provides compelling evidence of the drug's efficacy.

_ Reduced Risk of Death: Of the 731 participants with diastolic heart failure and a BMI of 30 or above, only 36 patients receiving tirzepatide died or suffered worsening heart failure, compared to 56 in the placebo group.
_ Weight Loss: Patients receiving tirzepatide lost, on average, 11.6% of their body weight, contributing to overall health improvement.
_ Improved Heart Function: MRI scans showed reductions in left ventricular mass and surrounding fat tissue, improving heart structure and function.

+ Implications for Heart Failure Treatment
_ Targeting Obesity and Heart Failure: Obesity is a key risk factor for diastolic heart failure, which affects nearly half of all heart failure cases. Tirzepatide’s effects on both weight and heart function make it a promising treatment for patients with this condition.
_ Beyond Weight Loss: The study emphasizes that tirzepatide offers more than just weight loss—it actively improves heart health, reduces hospitalization rates, and boosts patients' quality of life.

+ Potential Side Effects
_ Gastrointestinal Issues: Mild to moderate side effects, such as nausea and diarrhea, were reported in some participants but were generally manageable.

+ Expert Insights
_ Dr. Christopher Kramer, the chief of UVA Health’s Division of Cardiovascular Medicine, highlighted the broader benefits of tirzepatide, stating that the drug will become a crucial part of treatment for obesity-related heart failure and preserved heart function.

+ Conclusion
_ This study adds to growing evidence that tirzepatide, sold under the brand name Zepbound, is not only effective for weight loss but also provides substantial cardiovascular benefits for patients with obesity-related heart failure. 
_ The drug's ability to improve heart function and reduce mortality could redefine treatment strategies for this population.

Blinding is certainly broken for many patients experiencing "abnormal" weight loss, which at some degree could lead to bias. But you'd need a explain exactly why it is likely for the net bias to favorably affect the intervention and not the control.

The reason being: there are other sources of bias that could go against tirzepatide.

One of the most obvious is what happens in any weight loss trial:

The greater the weight lost, the greater is the tendency to need (and therefore receive) less medications.

TLDR:

1. Weight loss causes the intervention group to receive less medicine than the control group

2. Comparison is NOT "more weight loss vs. less weight loss"

3. Comparison is "more weight loss + less meds vs. less weight loss + more meds"

4. Therefore, the benefits of weight loss is partially counterbalanced by meds

Distribution challenges remain due to complex supply chain needs but are being managed with increased supply investments.
🏥 Major Investments in Manufacturing Capacity

Lilly announced a nearly $2 billion investment in Ireland to expand manufacturing, bringing total commitments to $20 billion since 2020.
A separate $4.5 billion initiative, the Lilly Medicine Foundry, will be built in Indiana for R&D and manufacturing process design to accelerate medicine delivery.
💸 Financial Performance Highlights

Gross margin increased to 82.2%, driven by favorable product mix and higher realized prices.
R&D expenses rose 13% with a continued push in both early and late-stage pipelines, and operating income reached nearly $1.8 billion, led by new product revenue growth.
Q3 EPS was $1.19, including a significant negative impact from acquired IPR&D charges, reflecting ongoing acquisitions like Morphic Therapeutics.
🌐 Expansion in International Markets

Revenue in Europe grew 39% in constant currency (excluding the olanzapine divestiture), mainly from Mounjaro, Verzenio, and Jardiance.
Mounjaro launches in countries such as the U.K., Germany, Spain, and Italy are contributing to strong global demand.
In emerging markets, growth is notable, particularly in China and Japan, driven by Humalog, Tauvid, and Verzenio.

New Phase II and Phase III studies in areas like immunology and cardiometabolic health demonstrate Lilly’s expansion into chronic disease treatments and potential disease-modifying therapies.
💼 Product Approvals and Launches

Progress in global access and commercialization for products like Verzenio, Mounjaro, and Zepbound has been strong, with several approvals and ongoing discussions with payers.
📊 2024 Financial Guidance Update

Three quarters of Americans are overweight or obese. Only 5% will ever lose weight with diet and exercise. Are drugs the only real solution to the obesity epidemic?

David Friedberg recently dug into that and more in an interview with Eli Lilly CEO Dave Ricks.

GLP-1’s for Weight Loss

Lilly was one of the first companies to make a GLP-1 drug available for weight loss. These drugs, which were originally developed for diabetes, are also highly effective in treating obesity.

GLP-1’s, such as Ozempic and Mounjaro, basically make your body think it’s full when it’s not. This means you eat less and lose weight.

People on GLP-1’s tend have less interest in overeating or fattening foods. A study by Wal-Mart found that shoppers on GLP-1’s bought food with 1/3 fewer calories, in particular reducing their consumption of salty snacks.

In my 20’s, I lost 70 pounds purely through diet and exercise. You can definitely lose weight without drugs.

But the reality is, most people just aren’t going to do that. For most, pharmaceuticals may be the only realistic option.

The Everything Drug?

GLP-1’s can help people lose weight. But there’s early evidence that they’re useful for other compulsions as well.

Animal studies suggest that the drugs could help people addicted to alcohol or opioids. The medicines seem to cause animals to lose interest in alcohol or opioids, much like humans became less interested in potato chips.

There’s even evidence in humans that patients on GLP-1’s are less likely to become depressed.

Given how many common conditions GLP-1’s can address, I expect to see half of Americans taking one within the next 10-20 years. Already, some insurers are changing their actuarial tables, expecting people to live longer as a result of these medications.

The Drugs of the Future

As incredible as GLP-1’s are, they come with some barriers. For now, they must be injected. And if you stop taking them, you will probably gain the weight back.

Lilly is working to fix these issues. They’re developing a pill version of a GLP-1. They’re also working on weight loss drugs that you’d only need to take for a limited time.

Ricks and his team are also working on another incredible project: a medication to lower Lp(a). Lp(a) is a biomarker that is closely associated with cardiovascular disease.

If a drug can lower your levels of Lp(a), your risk of death from cardiovascular disease could plummet.

This condition is the biggest killer in America. Preventing it could significantly increase life expectancy.

Wrap-Up

Eli Lilly was founded in 1876. It started out as a tiny little workshop. You wouldn’t know if they were making medicines or bicycles.

Today, it’s the largest pharmaceutical company on earth by market cap, worth over $800 billion. More importantly, Lilly is producing drugs that save countless lives.

Seeing that tiny little workshop, I’m put in mind of this quote from Jeff Bezos:

“Big things start small.”

🚨 The Seed Oil - Obesity Connection: What You Need to Know 🚨

There’s growing evidence suggesting that seed oils, may play a significant role in disrupting metabolic health. One theory points to their negative impact on GLP-1 production, a crucial hormone that regulates blood sugar and appetite.

GLP-1 helps control blood glucose levels by stimulating insulin secretion, slowing gastric emptying, and reducing appetite. These effects are precisely why drugs like Ozempic and Mounjaro, which increase GLP-1 levels, have become blockbuster treatments for diabetes and weight loss.

But here’s the problem… seed oils may do the opposite. By blocking or impairing GLP-1 production, seed oils could reduce insulin secretion efficiency, worsen blood sugar control, and even increase appetite… potentially leading to overeating and weight gain. In essence, seed oils might undermine the very mechanisms that GLP-1 targeting drugs are designed to enhance.

This raises important questions about the widespread use of seed oils in processed foods and their potential role in the obesity and diabetes epidemics. While Ozempic and Mounjaro aim to fix a broken system by boosting GLP-1, seed oils may be a key factor in why the system is broken in the first place. Could eliminating or significantly reducing seed oils from the diet help improve metabolic health naturally, without relying on medications? It’s a question worth exploring as we continue to uncover the impact of ultra-processed foods on our bodies.

How the SH2B1 Gene Influences Obesity: Potential Pathways to New Treatments

+ Research Background: 
Obesity is a complex condition influenced by various factors, including genetics, environment, and behavior. Among the many genetic contributors to obesity, the SH2B1 gene has been identified as a critical regulator of food intake and energy expenditure. Mutations in this gene are associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (formerly known as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease).

+ Key Findings: 
Researchers at the University of Michigan Medical School, led by Dr. Liangyou Rui, have discovered that the SH2B1 gene plays a significant role in the brain's regulation of body weight. Specifically, SH2B1 is active in the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVH), a brain region responsible for regulating blood pressure, fluid balance, and appetite. The study revealed that SH2B1-expressing neurons in the PVH communicate with neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN), a brainstem area involved in energy balance, body weight maintenance, and emotion-motivated behavior.

By stimulating this neuronal circuit in mice, the researchers were able to suppress appetite, while silencing these neurons led to obesity. This suggests that SH2B1 is crucial for maintaining a healthy balance between food intake and energy expenditure.

+ Molecular Mechanism: 
The study also uncovered that SH2B1 enhances BDNF/TrkB signaling—a pathway vital for brain development and health. Disruptions in this signaling, potentially due to inflammation from weight gain, can lead to obesity and metabolic diseases. The conservation of SH2B1 across species, from fruit flies to humans, highlights its fundamental role in regulating appetite and metabolism.

+ Implications for Treatment: 
Enhancing SH2B1 activity presents a promising avenue for treating obesity and related diseases. Unlike current popular drugs like Ozempic or Mounjaro, which activate GLP-1 receptors and come with side effects, boosting SH2B1 has shown no adverse effects so far. This finding could pave the way for new treatments that target SH2B1, offering effective solutions for metabolic diseases with fewer side effects.

+ Expert Insight: 
Dr. Rui emphasized the importance of SH2B1 in regulating appetite and metabolism, noting that its enhancement could offer significant potential for treating obesity without the drawbacks of current medications. As research continues, targeting SH2B1 could lead to safer and more effective obesity treatments.
